raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Motivation

Several `sglang serve` processes on one host each materialize the **same** layerwise pinned host store. For MiniMax-H3 fl2va that store is 108.5 GiB of page-locked host memory (transformer 62.28 GB + text encoder 46.18 GB), while each server uses only ~10 GiB of a 96 GiB card — so the host, not VRAM, is what limits how many can run.

Part of that duplication is already handled: `main`'s read-only checkpoint mapping shares page-cache pages across processes (36.7 GiB per instance at N=2 in the run below). What cannot be shared that way is the **pinned** store, because `cudaHostRegister` refuses a read-only file mapping, a writable one breaks copy-on-write per process, and `_shared_storage` is an anonymous memfd that peers cannot open.

Measured on `main` with sharing off, one server per GPU started one at a time, on an otherwise idle 498 GiB host (build and its one caveat in *Speed Tests* below): the first server costs 126 GiB of host memory and **every further one costs another ~123 GiB**. Two servers already need 249 GiB and four need ~496 GiB, so four co-resident servers are not reachable today.

## Modifications

Name the segment so a peer can attach to the creator's copy:

- The first instance creates, fills and registers the segment, then publishes a per-store marker.
- A follower waits for that marker, attaches, compares the store against the weights **it** loaded from disk, and only then registers it in its own CUDA context. A store holding different bytes is refused and the caller allocates privately, so a mismatch costs memory rather than correctness.

Ownership uses two independent locks, neither ever converted (POSIX does not make `flock` conversion atomic):

- `<base>.owner` — held exclusively for life by the creator;
- `<base>.users` — held shared for life by every process serving a generation;
- `<base>.decide` — a short mutex that serialises the decision.

Reclaiming a generation requires holding **both** locks exclusively at once, which is only possible once no creator and no follower is alive, so the kernel answers "is anyone still serving?" instead of a wall clock. The participant that leaves last runs that same check on its way out, under the same `.decide` mutex, and releases the generation there — stopping the servers returns the memory instead of leaving it for a next start that may never come. That exit is a signal, not a return: a unit stops with `KillMode=control-group`, so SIGTERM reaches the worker directly and no `atexit`/finalizer runs, which is why the release hangs off a handler (and why the handler refuses to re-enter: a stop delivers that signal more than once, and an inner call re-raising it would kill the process in the middle of the release the outer one is running). A process killed with `SIGKILL` reaches no handler at all; its generation is left for the next creator, which reclaims it exactly as before. Both the create and the attach path unregister the segment from the resource tracker: `SharedMemory.__init__` registers on attach too, and the tracker unlinks what it registered when its process exits.

The decision wraps the existing `_prepare_host_buffer` call and reuses its `populated` flag, so the private path is byte-for-byte what it was. Everything is behind `SGLANG_DIFFUSION_SHARE_PINNED_STORES`, default off, so the existing layerwise tests (which monkeypatch `_shared_storage` / `_pin_in_place`) are unaffected.

## Accuracy Tests

No model-output change: the store is compared byte-for-byte against the weights each process loaded before it is used, and a mismatch falls back to a private allocation. Verified on hardware that owner and follower produce identical output for the same seed, and that all four co-resident instances still complete requests with the pool shared.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No speed claim. This is a host-memory capacity change.

Same build, same GPUs, same payload, no other server resident; one instance per GPU, started one at a time, `Pss` read 30 s after `/health` returns. The only variable is `SGLANG_DIFFUSION_SHARE_PINNED_STORES`.

The build is this change plus the LoRA-merge-cache read-only change from #43261. That one is separate and this PR does not depend on it, but it is what makes the 62 GiB merged-weight cache shared; on a checkout of this PR alone the cache is privately mapped per process, both columns below are ~43 GiB higher per instance (measured in #43261), and the per-instance difference between the columns is the 108.5 GiB pinned store either way.

| N | sharing off | host added by this instance | sharing on | host added by this instance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 197.32 GiB | +126 GiB | 197.52 GiB | +127 GiB |
| 2 | 158.61 GiB | +123 GiB | 106.56 GiB | **+18 GiB** |
| 3 | — | — | 76.24 GiB | **+12 GiB** |
| 4 | — | — | **60.93 GiB** | **+18 GiB** |

(measured before the last-exit release landed; the numbers are the same store either way)

With sharing off the second instance adds a second 108.5 GiB store of its own; the run was stopped there rather than driving the host into reclaim. N=4 for that column is the measured per-instance cost extrapolated (~496 GiB), not a run — it does not fit next to a 498 GiB machine's other users.

With sharing on, four instances reach steady state at 54.53 / 60.76 / 60.74 / 60.83 GiB Pss, `/dev/shm` stays at 108 GiB with 129 segments, every process reports `deleted=0`, and the host still has 211 GiB available — 175 GiB total for four servers that previously needed ~496 GiB. All four pools log `follower, created 0, joined 2 / 50 / 27, refused 0`.

Lifecycle checks on the same build: killing the owner leaves the followers serving (`/dev/shm` unchanged, a real request still completes); restarting it logs `follower` and re-attaches the same segment with zero reclaims.

## Known limitations

- **Only layers the pin planner pinned are shared.** The join happens inside the `pin_this_layer` branch, and `main`'s host budget is derived from what is *available* when the plan is made. A follower on an already-busy host is therefore told to demote part of a component to `pageable`, and those layers get a private copy instead of joining the store. Measured with another server holding 108 GiB of pinned memory: the follower saw 77.8 GiB available and hosted 38 of 50 text-encoder layers pageable (35.99 GB private, against 1.45 GB when the host is quiet). Attaching to a store that is already registered should not be charged against the local pin budget; that is a follow-up, and until it lands the saving holds on a host that is otherwise quiet.
- The store key is structural (`component:layer_idx:dtype:total_numel`) — the manager cannot see checkpoint or LoRA identity, so correctness rests on the byte comparison and a mismatch is a silent private allocation rather than an error.
- Opt-in and default off; no default-on claim.
- A clean exit is released by the last participant to leave. A unit stop is released from a signal handler: systemd stops with `KillMode=control-group`, so SIGTERM reaches the worker directly and no exit hook would run. Only a process killed with `SIGKILL` reaches neither, and its generation stays until the next creator reclaims it — both paths are covered by the CPU test.
- Benefit is specific to **discrete** GPUs. Where `device_shares_host_memory()` is true (GB10, Jetson), `main` keeps every layer on its mapping and there is no pinned copy to share, so the gain is zero.
- No end-to-end test on a device — see below.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). — all hooks pass on the changed files.
- [x] Add unit tests — `test/registered/unit/multimodal_gen/test_shared_pinned_store_lifetime.py` runs the pool lifetime on CPU in real child processes: owner election, a participant that leaves early reclaiming nothing, the last participant releasing the generation, the same release when the last one is SIGTERMed rather than returning, a killed participant leaving it to the next creator, and a store being trusted only after the bytes agree (`begin` with a refusing verifier falls back private). `commit()` needs a device, so the test writes the creator's marker directly and does not exercise registration; the four-instance runs above cover that.
- [x] Update documentation — `SGLANG_DIFFUSION_SHARE_PINNED_STORES` added to `docs/docs/sglang-diffusion/environment_variables.mdx`.
- [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results — memory only, see above; no speed or accuracy delta claimed.
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

## Review and Merge Process

Given the lifetime semantics here, I would rather agree on the direction before this is reviewed in detail — the related open report is #36853, where the same host-memory duplication appears between SP ranks of one engine. Happy to split, re-scope, or drop this in favour of the stagger/shard options listed there if that is the preferred direction.

+"""Named pinned host stores that co-resident instances serve from one copy.
+
+The layerwise offload weight store has to be anonymous shared memory: it is the
+only form cudaHostRegister accepts that can also be shared between processes.
+sglang creates it with an anonymous memfd, so every instance on the host gets
+its own copy of the whole component -- 62.28 GB for H3's transformer, 46.18 GB
+for its text encoder.
+
+Naming the segment turns those into one copy per component. Three things have
+to hold for that to be stable, and each of them was learned the hard way:
+
+1. The name has to outlive the creating process's tracker.
+   `multiprocessing.SharedMemory(create=True)` registers the segment with a
+   resource_tracker, which unlinks everything it registered when its process
+   exits. In a serve process tree that tracker belongs to a short-lived parent,
+   so the segments were unlinked while the creator was still serving: a later
+   instance found the name free, created a second full pool under the same
+   names, and the first pool survived only as unreachable pages. /dev/shm held
+   two 109 GiB generations, and the two instances shared nothing. Every create
+   now unregisters itself (Python 3.12 has no `track=False`).
+
+2. A generation may only be replaced when nothing is reading it.
+   Two locks answer that, and neither is ever converted:
+     <base>.owner  held exclusively for its whole life by the one process that
+                   is allowed to create a generation
+     <base>.users  held shared for its whole life by every process serving a
+                   generation
+   Reclaiming the segments requires holding both exclusively at once, which is
+   only possible when no creator and no follower is alive. A short-lived
+   <base>.decide mutex serialises the decision itself, so the users lock can be
+   tested and dropped without a race.
+   An earlier version had the creator hold one lock exclusively and followers
+   take that same lock shared -- which flock refuses. The followers fell
+   through to a lockless join, and the next creator went on to unlink a
+   generation three live instances were still reading.
+
+3. A generation has to be reclaimed, and only one process may ever do it.
+   Holding both locks proves there are no participants left, so the creator
+   unlinks the previous generation's segments -- listed in a manifest -- before
+   creating its own. Without this the orphaned pages stay until reboot.
+   A named segment also outlives its readers, so the participant that leaves
+   last runs the same check on its way out and unlinks the generation there,
+   rather than leaving the whole component to a next start that may never come.
+   Leaving is either a signal -- a unit stops with SIGTERM to every process in
+   it, so the release runs from a handler -- or a return, which a
+   multiprocessing child makes through `os._exit` and a finalizer. SIGKILL
+   reaches neither, and the next creator reclaims instead.
+
+   create    the creator allocates each segment, fills it, registers it, then
+             publishes its marker.
+   attach    a follower waits for the marker before opening the segment, so it
+             can never read a half-filled store, and waits for one the creator
+             has not reached yet instead of allocating a second copy.
+   verify    the follower compares the store against the weights *it* loaded
+             from disk. The key only has to be structural, because a store
+             holding different bytes is rejected rather than trusted.
+   miss      the creator stopped advancing, or the bytes differ: the follower
+             closes the segment and its caller allocates privately.
+"""
+
+import ctypes
+import fcntl
+import hashlib
+import logging
+import os
+import signal
+import time
+from multiprocessing import resource_tracker, shared_memory, util
+
+import torch
+
+logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
+
+MARKER_DIR = "/tmp/sglang-shared-stores"
+
+# A creator that is alive but slow -- CPU-starved, or faulting its first layer
+# off a cold network mount -- keeps advancing, so followers keep waiting. Only
+# a creator with no progress for this long is given up on.
+STALL_TIMEOUT_S = 90.0
+MAX_WAIT_S = 900.0
+
+# The decision covers unlinking a whole dead generation, which is fast; a peer
+# stuck here is a peer that will never finish.
+DECIDE_TIMEOUT_S = 120.0
+
+_LIVE: dict[str, shared_memory.SharedMemory] = {}
+_LOCKS: dict[str, list[int]] = {}
+_ROLE: dict[str, bool | None] = {}
+_FILLED: dict[str, int] = {}
+_STATS: dict[str, dict[str, int]] = {}
+_LEAVING: set[str] = set()
+_TERM_HOOKED = False
+_RELEASING = False

+and register it. This drives the lifetime half -- who owns a generation, who
+may replace it, and who releases it -- through `join_pool` / `leave_pool` in
+real child processes, which needs no GPU.

+open by the parent until the parent says otherwise, so every check below sees
+one arrangement at a time:

+  * a participant that leaves while another is still serving reclaims nothing;

+        """The exit that actually happens in a deployment: a signal, not a return.
+
+        A unit stops with SIGTERM to every process in its cgroup, so the worker
+        never reaches `atexit` or a finalizer. The last participant still has to
+        release the generation from the handler, or the whole component stays in
+        /dev/shm until some later start.
+        """
+        pool = _pool_name()
+        keys = _keys(pool)
+        names = [store._names(key)[0] for key in keys]
+        owner = follower = None
+        try:

+            follower = _start(tmp_path, _serve, pool, keys)
+            _release(*owner[:2])
+            owner = None
+            assert _present(names), "a clean return released the pool too early"
+
+            follower[0].terminate()
+            follower[0].join(timeout=DEADLINE_S)
+            follower = None
+            assert not any(os.path.exists(_segment_path(n)) for n in names), (
+                "the last participant was signalled but did not release the generation"
+            )
+        finally:
+            if owner is not None:
+                _release(*owner[:2])
+            if follower is not None:
+                _release(*follower[:2])
+            _clear(pool)
